BenignTraffic: Normal, legitimate traffic produced by everyday device and user activity, such as web browsing, DNS lookups, media streaming and routine IoT device check-ins. It usually shows complete TCP handshakes, balanced request and response patterns, and moderate packet rates. It does not contain floods, scans or malicious payloads.
Backdoor_Malware: Malware that gives an attacker hidden remote access to a compromised device, bypassing normal authentication. On the network it often appears as unexpected outbound connections to a command-and-control server, or a device listening on unusual ports. Traffic is typically low in volume but persistent, with periodic beaconing and occasional bursts when commands or data are exchanged.
BrowserHijacking: An attack that takes control of how a browser behaves, for example by injecting malicious scripts or altering content so the victim lands on attacker-chosen pages. On the network it shows up as web requests that are redirected or modified, often involving unexpected domains or injected content in HTTP responses. The goal is usually to steal data, show unwanted content or lead users to further malicious sites.
CommandInjection: An attack in which the attacker sends crafted input to a vulnerable application so that the underlying system runs operating system commands. On the network it looks like web requests whose parameters contain shell separators or command strings. If it succeeds, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the target device.
DDoS-ACK_Fragmentation: A distributed denial-of-service attack in which many sources send large numbers of fragmented TCP ACK packets at a target. The ACKs do not belong to any real connection, and the fragments force the target to spend resources reassembling them. The result is a heavy packet load that can exhaust the target's processing capacity or bandwidth.
DDoS-HTTP_Flood: A distributed attack in which many sources send a very large number of HTTP requests, such as GET or POST, to a web server. Each request can look like normal web traffic, but the combined volume uses up the server's connections and processing power. On the network it appears as a sudden surge of HTTP requests to one target from many addresses.
DDoS-ICMP_Flood: A distributed attack where many sources send a flood of ICMP packets, typically echo requests (pings), to a target. The target has to process and often answer each one, which consumes bandwidth and CPU. On the network it appears as an abnormally high rate of ICMP traffic arriving at one destination from many sources.
DDoS-ICMP_Fragmentation: A distributed attack that sends large numbers of fragmented ICMP packets to a target from many sources. The target must buffer and try to reassemble the fragments, which ties up memory and processing resources. Traffic appears as a high volume of ICMP fragments that never form useful, complete exchanges.
DDoS-PSHACK_Flood: A distributed attack that floods a target with TCP packets that have the PSH and ACK flags set, from many sources. These flags tell the receiver to pass data up to the application right away and acknowledge it, so each packet creates extra work. The sheer volume of such packets can overwhelm the target's network stack and resources.
DDoS-RSTFINFlood: A distributed attack that sends huge numbers of TCP packets with the RST and FIN flags set, which normally end or reset connections. The packets usually do not match any real session, but the target still spends effort inspecting and handling them. On the network it appears as a large volume of connection-termination packets aimed at one host.
DDoS-SYN_Flood: A distributed attack in which many sources send a large number of TCP SYN packets to start connections but never complete the handshake. The target keeps half-open connections waiting for the final step, which fills its connection table. On the network it shows up as a very high rate of SYN packets with few or no completed connections.
DDoS-SlowLoris: A low-bandwidth denial-of-service technique, here launched from many sources, that opens many connections to a web server and keeps them alive by sending incomplete HTTP requests very slowly. The server holds each connection open waiting for the rest, until it runs out of available connections. On the network it looks like many long-lived connections with tiny, infrequent amounts of data rather than a big traffic spike.
DDoS-SynonymousIP_Flood: A distributed attack that sends packets whose source and destination IP addresses are the same, typically the target's own address. Such packets are abnormal and can confuse the target's network stack or make it respond to itself, wasting resources. On the network it appears as a high volume of packets with matching source and destination addresses.
DDoS-TCP_Flood: A distributed attack in which many sources send an overwhelming number of TCP packets to a target. The target must process every packet and maintain state for connection attempts, which consumes bandwidth and CPU. On the network it appears as a sustained, abnormally high rate of TCP traffic toward one destination from many addresses.
DDoS-UDP_Flood: A distributed attack in which many sources send a very large number of UDP packets to a target, often to many different ports. Because UDP is connectionless, the target has to check each packet and may reply with ICMP unreachable messages, using up resources. On the network it appears as a heavy surge of UDP traffic aimed at a single host.
DDoS-UDP_Fragmentation: A distributed attack that sends large numbers of fragmented UDP packets to a target from many sources. The target spends memory and processing power trying to reassemble fragments that never form useful messages. Traffic appears as a high volume of UDP fragments directed at one destination.
DNS_Spoofing: An attack in which forged DNS responses are sent so that a victim resolves a legitimate domain name to an IP address chosen by the attacker. This can redirect users to fake sites or intercept their traffic. On the network it appears as unexpected or conflicting DNS replies, often answering faster than the real server or pointing to unusual addresses.
DictionaryBruteForce: A password-guessing attack that tries many likely passwords from a prepared word list against a login service such as SSH, Telnet, FTP or a web login. On the network it appears as many repeated authentication attempts from one source in a short time, mostly failing. The goal is to find valid credentials and gain access to the device.
DoS-HTTP_Flood: A denial-of-service attack in which a single source sends a large number of HTTP requests to a web server. The requests look like ordinary web traffic, but the volume exhausts the server's connections and processing capacity. On the network it appears as a rapid stream of HTTP requests from one address to one target.
DoS-SYN_Flood: A denial-of-service attack in which one source sends a rapid stream of TCP SYN packets without completing the handshake. The target keeps half-open connections waiting, which eventually fills its connection table. On the network it appears as a very high rate of SYN packets from a single address with few completed connections.
DoS-TCP_Flood: A denial-of-service attack in which a single source sends an overwhelming number of TCP packets to a target. The target must handle each packet and any connection state it creates, using up bandwidth and CPU. On the network it appears as a sustained, abnormally high rate of TCP traffic from one address to one destination.
DoS-UDP_Flood: A denial-of-service attack in which a single source sends a very large number of UDP packets to a target, often across many ports. The target has to process each packet and may send back ICMP unreachable messages, which consumes resources. On the network it appears as a heavy burst of UDP traffic from one address to one host.
MITM-ArpSpoofing: A man-in-the-middle attack in which the attacker sends forged ARP messages to link their own MAC address with another device's IP address, often the gateway. Traffic meant for that device is then sent through the attacker, who can read or alter it. On the network it appears as unsolicited or conflicting ARP replies and an IP address that suddenly maps to a different MAC address.
Mirai-greeth_flood: A flood launched by devices infected with Mirai botnet malware, using GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) packets that carry Ethernet frames. The target must process large numbers of these encapsulated packets, which consumes bandwidth and processing resources. On the network it appears as a high volume of GRE traffic aimed at one destination.
Mirai-greip_flood: A flood launched by devices infected with Mirai botnet malware, using GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) packets that carry IP packets inside. The target has to unwrap and handle each one, which wastes bandwidth and processing power. On the network it appears as a heavy stream of GRE traffic directed at a single target.
Mirai-udpplain: A UDP flood launched by devices infected with Mirai botnet malware, using simple UDP packets with little or no special crafting. The goal is to saturate the target's bandwidth or processing capacity with sheer volume. On the network it appears as a high rate of plain UDP packets, often with similar sizes, sent to one destination.
Recon-HostDiscovery: A reconnaissance activity that probes a network to find out which devices are online, using requests such as ARP, ICMP or simple TCP probes. It does not attack the hosts directly but maps what is present for later attacks. On the network it appears as many short probes sent to a range of addresses, with replies revealing which hosts are active.
Recon-OSScan: A reconnaissance technique that sends specially crafted packets to a device and studies how it responds in order to guess its operating system. Differences in how systems handle certain packets and options act as a fingerprint. On the network it appears as a series of unusual or varied probes to one host, often combined with port probing.
Recon-PingSweep: A reconnaissance technique that sends ICMP echo requests (pings) to a whole range of IP addresses to see which ones answer. It is a simple way to list live hosts on a network. On the network it appears as a rapid sequence of ping requests to consecutive addresses from one source.
Recon-PortScan: A reconnaissance technique that tries to connect to many ports on a target to find which are open and which services are running. It is usually an early step before an attack on a discovered service. On the network it appears as many short connection attempts from one source to numerous different ports on the same host, often with many refused or unanswered.
SqlInjection: An attack in which malicious SQL code is placed into input fields or request parameters of a web application so the back-end database runs it. It can expose, change or delete stored data, or bypass login checks. On the network it appears as web requests whose parameters contain SQL keywords, quotes and special characters.
Uploading_Attack: An attack in which the attacker uploads a malicious file, such as a script or web shell, to a vulnerable web application or device. If the server accepts and runs the file, the attacker can gain control over it. On the network it appears as HTTP upload requests carrying unexpected file types or content, often followed by requests to run the uploaded file.
VulnerabilityScan: An automated process that probes a device or service to look for known weaknesses such as outdated software or misconfigurations. It is often a preparation step before an actual exploit. On the network it appears as many varied requests to different ports and services from one source in a short time, often using patterns typical of scanning tools.
XSS: Cross-site scripting, an attack in which malicious script code is inserted into a web page or request so that it runs in another user's browser. It can be used to steal session data, redirect users or change what the page shows. On the network it appears as web requests or responses containing script tags or encoded script content in parameters.
